title: Big super loses governance ace in mystery exit
full_text:
The Australian Council of Superannuation Investors' key governance adviser has abruptly left on the eve of the annual shareholder meeting season, leading to disquiet among major retirement savings funds as the group's chief executive refuses to explain the reason for his departure.
Known as ACSI, the organisation helps the country's major superannuation funds - including AustralianSuper, HESTA, Hostplus, Aware Super and Cbus - decide how to vote on resolutions put to shareholders in ASX-listed companies. The body is chaired by IFM Investors' head of external relations David Whiteley; its long-time chief executive is Louise Davidson.
Ed John had been ACSI's executive manager of stewardship, overseeing many of its recommendations, from shortly after it was established in 2001, and was described by one super fund official who spoke on condition of anonymity as the "real brains of the operation" and a trusted adviser.
ACSI confirmed John had departed in August, but declined to comment on the reasons for his departure. John has also been contacted for comment, but not has responded.
There has been considerable support for John on LinkedIn, with UniSuper's manager of ESG investing, Jodie Barns, writing that he had gone "on to become one of the most recognisable and respected voices in corporate governance and stewardship".
"There's a lot of talk about the legacy of ACSI's founders Phil Spathis and Michael O'Sullivan. But Ed is a huge part of that too. In many ways, ACSI's story is the story of all three," she wrote.
A farewell event for John was held at a Melbourne bar last month, although neither Whiteley nor Davidson attended the function. The event's bar tab was picked up by Ownership Matters, a governance advisory that provides ACSI with research papers into companies that super funds own.
In an email to members in August, Davidson thanked John for his work at ACSI but provided no explanation for his departure.
"We thank Ed sincerely for his dedication, expertise and service and wish him every success for the future. I recognise that many of you have worked closely with Ed for many years, and the departure of a respected senior leader is naturally significant for the organisation. Members can be confident that stewardship activities will continue uninterrupted," she said.
Still, there has been growing frustration from some members behind the scenes at Whiteley and Davidson's international travels, as first reported in The Australian Financial Review's Rear Window column this week.
There is also disquiet among ACSI members about the fees charged by the organisation, with some paying up to $500,000 per year. Some have suggested that various industry bodies could be consolidated, privately floating the merger of ACSI with the Super Members Council.
Whiteley assumed the role of president in April, succeeding former HESTA chief executive Debby Blakey. The organisation's directors includes UniSuper's Lou Capparelli, Victorian Funds Management Corporation's Kate Galvin, Hostplus' Tim Lyons and Rest Super's Leilani Weier.
Two people briefed on the matter, who requested anonymity, said that Davidson raised the prospect of John leaving ACSI at a board meeting in late July. Some board members, including representatives of UniSuper, challenged the decision.
In a statement, an ACSI spokeswoman said: "Our hard-working stewardship team has deep company knowledge, strong relationships and sector expertise. They, and the organisation as a whole, remain focused on enhancing long-term investment outcomes and value for our members."
Davidson, a vocal champion of gender diversity, last year threatened to quit a corporate governance advisory council at the ASX if it dropped controversial diversity reporting for listed companies.
The ongoing deadlock resulted in the ASX scrapping the council and installing a new body, led by former Reserve Bank governor Phil Lowe. It is finalising a simplified version of the rules.
